messages.subject: INLA's biased output
parts:
Hi, 

I want to model a non-linear relationship using  a random walk model. Below is my approach: 

# simulate data
N = 100 # num of observations
x = sort(runif(N, -1 , 1)) # sort for line plot
eps = rnorm(N,0,.1)
fx = x^2 - x^3 + 2*x
y = fx + eps

df = data.frame(x=x, y=y)

# binning the predictor
df$x_binned = inla.group(df$x, n = 20, method = "cut")

# model definition
formula = y ~ f(x_binned, model = 'rw1')

# fitting the model
model = inla(formula, data = df, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))

# extracting the estimated effects
bin_id = model$summary.random$x_binned$ID
bin_mean = model$summary.random$x_binned$mean
post_pred = model$summary.fitted.values$mean

plot(x,y)
lines(bin_id, mean, col = 'red')
lines(x, post_pred, col = 'blue')

which results in the below plot: 



Does anyone know why the red line posterior mean of the bins is systematically underestimating the true values? What explains the gap between the two lines?

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA's biased output
parts:
Hi,

If you look at summary(model) I expect you’ll see that it added an intercept parameter to the model. That’s a feature of the R formula methods. I recommend explicitly controlling whether there should be an intercept or not:
Automatic intercept:
y ~ f(…)
Explicit intercept:
y ~ 1 + f(…)
No intercept:
y ~ 0 + f(…)   or   y ~ -1 + f(…)

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA's biased output
parts:
…and this is extra complicated for rw1 and similar models with improper distribution; inla automatically imposes a sum-to-zero constraint in some circumstances to avoid mutual non-identifiability with the intercept.

Finn
